source.title: Least Squares Regression Can Exhibit Under-Parameterized Double Descent

page_placements.theme: Predictor norms can peak at interpolation without uniquely predicting risk

record.tranche_reason: The study derives and experimentally illustrates double descent in under-parameterized least-squares settings, including a one-hidden-layer network, refining the claim that peaks occur only at or beyond interpolation. It also examines when peaks disappear and reports multiple peaks in one neural-network experiment.
record.gate_note: Rows record the paper's own risk outcomes and peak locations. The estimator-norm peak and training-error-derivative results are omitted because they are not test-error results. Cited findings from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper proves and simulates risk curves for linear least squares, plus one small neural-network experiment. Its own results show that the double-descent peak can sit inside the under-parameterized regime (c=1/(1+mu^2) or c=pi1) rather than at or beyond interpolation. It also shows when the peak disappears under regularization and reports multiple peaks. This argues that parts of V3, V4, V5 and V6 need restating, so T5.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors show two linear models with provable under-parameterized peaks, located at c=1/(1+mu^2) and c=pi1. Peak location depends on target-eigenvector alignment and on the Stieltjes transform of the spectrum. A norm peak need not imply a risk peak. They call such peaks seemingly limited to special cases and leave deep networks open.
record.recipe_differences: The paper gives theoretical and empirical studies of linear least squares and a limited one-hidden-layer neural-network denoising experiment, rather than reproducing the original deep-network size, epoch, or sample-size experiments. It varies aspect ratio and data structure, including input-noise and mixture settings.
record.method_sensitivity: Peak location and existence vary with ridge parameter mu, data-scaling versus parameter-scaling regime, covariance mixture weight, and whether MNIST is projected to a low-dimensional subspace. In the neural-network experiment the authors note multiple risk peaks and a mechanism different from the linear examples.

fits_no_version.finding: The estimator norm ||W_opt||_F peaks at c=1/(1+mu^2) even when the risk curve is monotonic (Theorem 3, Fig 5-6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A peak in estimator norm does not imply a peak in test risk.

fits_no_version.finding: Optimal ridge mu and optimal sigma_trn themselves show (inverted) double-descent curves as c varies (Fig 12, 14).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal regularization strength varies non-monotonically with aspect ratio.

record.problems: The principal results rely on specialized model and data assumptions and asymptotic theory. Empirical curves generally have no reported error bars or confidence intervals. The neural-network evidence is a single one-hidden-layer MNIST denoising setup, and the authors say generalization of the phenomena to other architectures remains open.
record.rows_left_out: Excluded estimator-norm peaks (Figures 5–6 and Theorem 3) and training-error/derivative results (Appendix C, Figure 10) because they are not test-error outcomes. Appendix D also includes parameter sweeps and optimal-parameter plots; only outcomes explicitly described as relevant to double descent or monotonic risk are retained (Figures 11 and 16).

untested.parts: No model-size sweep of deep networks.
No epoch-wise test-error curves; the NN is trained for a fixed 500 epochs.
Label/output-noise dependence of the peak is not varied. Only input noise and ridge are studied, apart from the closed-form mixture model.
No re-expression against an effective parameter count; Curth et al. is only cited.
No model classes beyond linear least squares, except the sample-wise NN experiment.

missing.what: Ablation: unregularized model with shifted noise spectrum keeps the peak at c=1. Replacing V-hat with a random orthogonal matrix moves the peak into the over-parameterized regime. This shows peak location is set by target alignment.
Training error vs peak location: no clear training-error signal in the ridge model, only a weak link to the third derivative. NN peaks match training-error local minima.
Mixture-model risk has its only peak at c=pi1 and descends beyond it (closed form, Theorem 4).

record.verdict_notes: The paper is not an original source. Most curves are theory-matched simulations without error bars. The NN experiment is a single setup. Rows R5 and R6 were re-linked from V4 to V6, and R7 dropped V4 because d is fixed.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep of deep networks testing a fall-peak-fall pattern near the size that just fits the training set.
The neural network is trained for 500 epochs, but the reported test-error sweep varies training-set size, not training epochs.
The study tests particular synthetic and denoising settings, not the generality of the effect across settings.
The study does not establish a general curve across model classes; its model-size evidence is limited to specified least-squares settings.
The study discusses alignment and spectrum as determinants of peak location but does not test whether a single effective-complexity measure predicts locations across axes.

The study does not test label-noise dependence or whether optimally tuned regularization eliminates peaks in general; it examines input-noise and ridge-regularized settings and reports a multiple-peak result.
No re-expression of the curve against an effective parameter count is tested; the related work is cited only.

relation.reason: The study proves and measures risk curves, peak locations, multiplicity, and regularization dependence.

tranche.reason: Own theoretical and empirical results qualify interpolation-based peak-location accounts and the connection between estimator-norm peaks and risk peaks.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is the October 2024 v3, identified as NeurIPS 2024. Exact risk-peak formulas must remain attached to their sweep; the neural-network experiment uses fixed regularization and supplies no optimized-removal test.

statements.correction: Theorem 2: fixed d, varying n, risk peak at c=1/(1+mu^2). Figure 4: fixed n, varying d, underparameterized risk peak for mu=0.1; exact location not stated. Theorem 3: parameter-scaling estimator-norm peak at c=1/(1+mu^2), subject to its assumptions.
statements.problem: The exact risk-peak formula is transferred from data scaling to parameter scaling.

statements.correction: Appendix C: ridge-model training error does not clearly signal the risk peak; a third-derivative minimum approximately tracks it. Section 5 and Appendix B: mixture-model and neural-network risk peaks coincide with training-error minima. No single effective-complexity predictor is evaluated.
statements.problem: The training-error findings are accurate, but they do not test prediction by a single effective-complexity measure across axes.

statements.correction: R12: optimizing sigma_trn at fixed mu leaves double descent. R13: joint optimization of sigma_trn and mu removes it. These results limit scope by regularizer choice. R14: fixed-mu variance/risk comparison.
statements.problem: The restricted-family result is accurate, but a challenges label overstates this study's evidence against optimal regularization generally; R14 is not an optimization experiment.
